lessons.title: Facial mechanics
lessons.objective: Learn to see individual facial movements before assigning emotion.
lessons.source_note: FACS-inspired; not a clinical coding exercise.
lessons.intro: Before a face can act, it has to move. This lesson slows down and isolates single facial movements — one brow, one eyelid, one lip corner at a time — so you can see the moving parts before you start naming emotions. Think of it as learning the alphabet before reading words.
lessons.exercise: Cover the mouth on the Brows plates and compare the three brow positions. What exactly changed?
lessons.exercise_answer: Look for the movement before the emotion: the inner ends rising, the outer ends rising, or the whole brow lowering and pulling together. Naming the movement first keeps you from jumping straight to a feeling word.

groups.title: Brows
groups.fixed: Keep eyes, lips and head angle neutral.
groups.learn: The eyebrows are the face's loudest single signal. By changing only which part of the brow moves — inner ends, outer ends, or the whole brow pulled down — you can suggest worry, openness or displeasure before anything else on the face changes.
observe: Inner brow raise: only the inner ends of the brows lift, leaving a peaked shape over the nose.
Outer brow raise: the outer ends lift while the inner ends stay level.
Brow lower: both brows drop and pull together, shadowing the eyes.
groups.meaning: Brow position alone can steer a neutral face toward concern, attentiveness or displeasure.
groups.alternatives: A lowered brow can also read as concentration, or as shading the eyes from bright light, so context decides.
groups.prompt_tip: Name the exact brow movement in your prompt — 'inner ends of the eyebrows raised' — instead of asking for an emotion word.

groups.title: Eyes and cheeks
groups.fixed: Keep eyebrows and mouth unchanged where anatomically possible.
groups.learn: The eyes change meaning through the lids and cheeks, not just the eyeballs. Raising the upper lids, lifting the cheeks, tightening the lids or simply blinking each shifts how alert, warm or guarded a face feels.
observe: Upper lid raise: the eyes open wider, showing more of the eye.
Cheek raise: the cheeks lift and the lower eyelids narrow from below.
Lid tighten and blink: the lids firm without closing, or close gently for a moment.
groups.meaning: Small lid and cheek movements control how open, engaged or at rest a face appears.
groups.alternatives: A blink is also a normal reflex, so a single closed-eye frame can read as calm or mid-speech rather than as an emotion.
groups.prompt_tip: Describe the eyelids directly — 'upper eyelids raised, eyes wide open' or 'cheeks lifted, lower eyelids narrowed' — rather than asking for 'expressive eyes'.

groups.title: Nose and upper lip
groups.fixed: Keep head and gaze fixed.
groups.learn: The middle of the face carries some of the strongest disgust signals. A wrinkled nose or a raised upper lip can flip a neutral expression toward distaste even when the eyes and jaw stay still.
observe: Nose wrinkle: the bridge and sides of the nose crease upward.
Upper lip raise: the upper lip lifts slightly while the jaw stays put.
In both plates the head and gaze stay fixed, so only the mid-face moves.
groups.meaning: Mid-face movements are the core physical ingredients of disgust and distaste.
groups.alternatives: A wrinkled nose can also appear when someone catches a strong smell or is about to sneeze, so it is not always social disgust.
groups.prompt_tip: Ask for the physical action — 'nose wrinkled, upper lip raised' — to get distaste without changing the whole face.

groups.title: Mouth
groups.fixed: Keep brows and gaze neutral.
groups.learn: The mouth is a whole instrument by itself: corners that pull up or down, lips that press, stretch, pucker or part. Learning these seven positions separately lets you build expressions deliberately instead of accepting whatever smile a generator hands you.
observe: Lip corner pull vs. depress: the corners rise in one plate and sink in the other.
Lip press, stretch and pucker: the lips flatten together, pull sideways, or push forward.
Chin raise and jaw drop: tension pushes the lower lip up in one plate; the jaw falls open in another.
groups.meaning: Mouth shape alone can carry the difference between pleasure, displeasure, tension and surprise.
groups.alternatives: A lip pucker can read as a kiss, a whistle or thoughtful doubt depending on the scene around it.
groups.prompt_tip: Specify the mouth mechanically — 'mouth corners pulled down, lips pressed flat' — and keep the rest of the face neutral in the same prompt.

lessons.title: Basic emotional expressions
lessons.objective: Recognize common expression families without treating them as universal diagnoses.
lessons.source_note: GoEmotions and EMOTIC inspired; curated examples.
lessons.intro: Now the individual movements combine into the expression families people recognize fastest: joy, anger, fear, sadness and their close relatives. These are common patterns, not universal diagnoses — the same face can be read differently in different cultures and situations.
lessons.exercise: Hide the labels and sort the expression plates into groups by similar visual cues. Then check your groups against the labels.
lessons.exercise_answer: More than one label may fit a face. Justify each grouping with features you can point to — brow position, lid openness and mouth shape — rather than with a gut feeling.

groups.title: Positive affect
groups.fixed: Same frontal framing and direct gaze.
groups.learn: Positive feelings are not one smile at different volumes. Amusement, joy, contentment and relief use different combinations of smile width, cheek lift and brow relaxation, and telling them apart makes a character's good moods specific.
observe: Amusement and joy: open or broad smiles with clearly lifted cheeks.
Contentment: a small, relaxed smile with soft eyes.
Relief: the smile softens and the brow relaxes, as if tension just left.
groups.meaning: The positive family ranges from active delight to the quiet release of tension, and the face marks each step.
groups.alternatives: A broad smile can also be performed for politeness or for a camera, so warmth is not guaranteed by the smile alone.
groups.prompt_tip: Pick the precise member of the family — 'small relaxed smile, soft eyes, contentment' — instead of the generic word 'happy'.

groups.title: Negative affect
groups.fixed: Same framing; expression only.
groups.learn: The negative expressions are built from the Lesson 1 parts working together: sadness raises the inner brows, anger lowers them, fear widens the eyes, disgust recruits the nose, and contempt breaks symmetry with a single raised corner.
observe: Sadness vs. anger: inner brows rise in one, while brows lower and lips tense in the other.
Fear and disgust: wide eyes and parted lips contrast with a wrinkled nose and raised upper lip.
Contempt: only one mouth corner rises, making the face deliberately uneven.
groups.meaning: Each negative emotion has a recognizable recipe, and the recipes differ in specific, nameable features.
groups.alternatives: These recipes are widely recognized but not universal diagnoses — display rules differ across cultures, and people often mask feelings in public.
groups.prompt_tip: Build the expression from parts — 'brows lowered and drawn together, eyes narrowed, lips pressed tense' for anger — rather than relying on the emotion label alone.

groups.title: Attention and surprise
groups.fixed: No symbols, props or lighting changes.
groups.learn: Some expressions are about reacting to the world rather than feeling an emotion: surprise, interest, confusion and boredom show how attention switches on, focuses, fails to resolve, or switches off.
observe: Surprise: brows up, eyes wide and jaw dropped all at once.

groups.meaning: Attention has a visible scale, from startled alertness down to disengagement.
groups.alternatives: Surprise is neutral about whether the news is good or bad — the same face can precede delight or alarm.

lessons.title: Complex and mixed emotions
lessons.objective: Show emotional distinctions with subtle facial cues.
lessons.source_note: GoEmotions-inspired; cues are artistic choices, not diagnostic rules.
lessons.intro: Real feelings rarely arrive one at a time. This lesson looks at emotions that depend on other people, on memory, or on two feelings pulling against each other — and at how small changes in the eyes, the gaze and the mouth carry those distinctions.
lessons.exercise: Put the Pride and Relief plates side by side. What makes them different?
lessons.exercise_answer: Compare head angle, gaze and mouth tension: pride lifts the chin with a restrained smile, while relief lets the brow relax and the breath out. If the difference is still hard to see, that is part of the lesson — some distinctions need context.

groups.title: Self-conscious emotions
groups.fixed: Do not change camera or costume.
groups.learn: Embarrassment, shame, pride and guilt are emotions about how we appear to others, and the face shows them through gaze direction and the chin as much as through the mouth: eyes avert, gaze drops, or the chin lifts.
observe: Embarrassment and shame: the eyes avert or the gaze lowers, with a small awkward smile or a tightened mouth.
Pride: the chin rises slightly with a restrained, contained smile.
Guilt: worried inner brows pair with pressed lips.
groups.meaning: Self-conscious emotions are written in where the face points and how much of it is offered to view.
groups.alternatives: A lowered gaze can signal respect or deference in many cultures rather than shame, so the social setting matters.
groups.prompt_tip: Combine gaze and chin with the feeling — 'gaze lowered, mouth tightened, ashamed' — because these emotions live in the head's direction.

groups.title: Social emotions

groups.title: Inner conflict
groups.fixed: Show ambiguity without text or icons.
groups.learn: Mixed emotions put two signals on one face at once: a smile with sad eyes, a tender smile with a distant gaze, steady eyes over parted anxious lips. This group shows how contradiction itself becomes the message.
observe: Bittersweet joy and nostalgia: smiles paired with moist, sad or distant eyes.
Disappointment and anxiety: a smile slackens as the gaze lowers, or tense brows sit over slightly parted lips.
Determination and disbelief: firm lips with steady eyes contrast with one raised brow and an open mouth.
groups.meaning: When the upper and lower face disagree, viewers read an inner conflict rather than a single clean emotion.
groups.alternatives: Mixed signals can also read as an unconvincing or posed expression, so the surrounding story decides whether viewers see depth or fakery.
groups.prompt_tip: Deliberately split the face in your prompt — 'smiling mouth but sad, moist eyes, bittersweet' — naming a different cue for the eyes and the mouth.

lessons.title: Emotional intensity and concealment
lessons.objective: Distinguish degree from type and outer display from inner feeling.
lessons.source_note: Curated intensity ladders.
lessons.intro: Emotions come in degrees, not just kinds: the same anger can simmer as irritation or boil over into fury, and the face changes gradually rather than switching on. This lesson trains you to read those steps — and to notice when the expression on the surface does not match the feeling underneath.
lessons.exercise: Put the anger ladder plates in intensity order from weakest to strongest, then point to the first subtle cue that tells you the feeling has begun.
lessons.exercise_answer: The order runs irritation, controlled anger, fury. The first cue is brow and jaw tension — a slight tightening around the brows and jaw appears long before the mouth opens, which shows that exaggeration is not the only way to show anger; the quiet end of the ladder is carried by small tensions.

groups.title: Anger ladder
groups.fixed: Keep head angle and lighting fixed.
groups.learn: Anger builds in steps, and the earliest step is easy to miss. Climb the ladder slowly and find the first plate where the feeling becomes visible at all.
observe: Irritation shows only slight brow tension — everything else stays neutral.
Controlled anger adds a tight jaw and lowered brows.

groups.title: Masking emotion
groups.fixed: No caption or thought bubble in the render.
groups.learn: People hide feelings, and the mask leaks. In each plate the mouth performs one emotion while the eyes, brows, or jaw quietly report another — learning to spot the mismatch is the whole skill.
observe: The polite smile pairs a smile with visibly tense eyes.
Forced confidence sets a firm smile against uneasy brows.
Suppressed tears show wet eyes above firmly pressed lips, and concealed anger hides behind an almost neutral mouth with a tight jaw and narrowed eyes.
groups.meaning: A displayed emotion can conceal a different felt emotion, and the concealed one leaks through the parts of the face the person controls least.
groups.alternatives: A tense polite smile is also just what tiredness or social awkwardness looks like — masking is a possibility to consider, not a lie detector.
concepts: Part II — tension around the eyes
Part III — mixed and concealed emotion
groups.prompt_tip: Prompt the mismatch directly: 'smiling politely but with tense eyes and a tight jaw' produces a masked expression instead of a simple one.

lessons.title: Gaze and attention
lessons.objective: Use eye direction and head orientation to imply intention.
lessons.source_note: Curated staging studies.
lessons.intro: Where a character looks tells the audience where the story is. A shift of the pupils or a turn of the head can signal interest, avoidance, or a thought the character never says out loud. This lesson separates eye direction from head orientation so you can use each one deliberately.
lessons.exercise: Cover the cup and the other props in the café plates with your hand. From the eyes and head alone, decide where her attention is in each plate.
lessons.exercise_answer: Follow the direction of the pupils and the orientation of the head: toward the table, toward the window, toward the entrance, or unfocused into the distance. Accept some uncertainty — when the gaze is unfocused or the target is outside the frame, the honest answer is a best guess, not a certainty.

groups.title: Eye direction
groups.fixed: Head fixed frontally; move only pupils.
groups.learn: The head never moves in this group — only the pupils do. Even so, each tiny shift redirects the character's attention, and yours with it.
observe: Pupils glance to image left, then to image right, with the head fixed frontally.
Pupils look up, then down, changing the feeling from searching to subdued.
The final plate looks away, gaze passing just beside the camera.
groups.meaning: Eye direction alone tells the audience what the character is attending to, without any head movement.
groups.alternatives: A sideways glance can read as shyness, suspicion, or simple distraction — pupil direction shows where attention goes, not why.
concepts: Part II — composition and off-frame space
groups.prompt_tip: Say where the pupils point: 'eyes glancing to the left, head facing forward' keeps the head still while moving the attention.

groups.title: Head orientation

lessons.title: Body language
lessons.objective: Understand posture as an expressive signal rather than a fixed diagnosis.
lessons.source_note: Danbooru posture vocabulary and curated acting cues.
lessons.intro: Long before we study a face, we read the body: open or closed, upright or slumped, still or restless. Posture is a strong signal, but it is a hint, not a diagnosis — the same crossed arms can mean defiance, cold, or simple comfort. This lesson compares postures side by side so you can see exactly what changes.
lessons.exercise: Cover her face with your thumb and, from the body alone, sort the plates into welcoming and defensive.
lessons.exercise_answer: Welcoming postures open the arms and keep the shoulders and torso open; defensive ones cross the arms, pull the shoulders inward, and close the torso off. If you can read the feeling with the face hidden, the posture is doing the storytelling.

groups.title: Openness and confidence
groups.fixed: Same full-body frame and floor marks.
groups.learn: Open postures take up space and expose the torso; reserved ones protect it. Compare how shoulders, arms, and feet change while the frame and costume stay identical.
observe: Confident stands upright with the torso open and shoulders relaxed back.
Assertive plants the feet apart with hands on hips; welcoming opens the arms with relaxed shoulders.
Reserved pulls the elbows close to the torso with hands loosely together.
groups.meaning: Openness of the torso and arms signals confidence and welcome; closing them signals reserve.
groups.alternatives: Hands on hips can read as impatient or confrontational rather than confident, depending on the face and the scene around her.
groups.prompt_tip: Describe the whole stance: 'standing tall, shoulders back, arms open in welcome' or 'elbows tucked in, hands clasped, reserved posture'.

groups.title: Defensive and vulnerable
groups.fixed: Neutral face, same costume.
groups.learn: Defensive postures build a barrier with the arms or shrink the body's outline. With the face kept neutral, the body alone has to carry the feeling — and it does.
observe: Defensive crosses the arms tightly over the chest.
Protective holds one arm across to grip the opposite elbow; timid turns the shoulders inward with feet close together.
Startled recoils the torso with raised shoulders.
groups.meaning: Crossed arms, inward shoulders, and recoil signal self-protection and vulnerability.
groups.alternatives: Crossed arms are also what people do when they are cold or simply comfortable, so treat the defensive reading as a first guess, not a verdict.
concepts: Part III — posture as signal, not diagnosis

groups.title: Energy and weight
groups.fixed: No environmental changes.
groups.learn: Energy shows in where the body's weight sits. Slumped, settled, forward-leaning — each distribution of weight suggests a different level of readiness and mood.
observe: Exhausted slumps the shoulders with drooping arms; dejected lowers the head and shoulders.
Relaxed rests the weight on one leg.
Restless shifts weight forward with tense feet, and determined squares the shoulders with forward weight.
groups.meaning: Weight distribution and shoulder line communicate energy, fatigue, and resolve.
groups.alternatives: A relaxed one-legged stance can also read as casual confidence, and slumped shoulders may mean a heavy bag or a long day rather than despair.
concepts: Part II — weight and balance in the figure

groups.title: Status contrast
groups.fixed: Same camera height; no size distortion.
groups.learn: Status is performed with the body: how centered, symmetrical, and still a stance is changes how much authority it claims. The camera height never changes here — the posture does all the work.
observe: Commanding stands upright and centered with hands behind the back.
Deferential bows slightly with hands together.
Rebellious breaks symmetry with an asymmetric stance and folded arms, while indifferent loosens the shoulders with one hand resting at the waist.
groups.meaning: Centered, upright stillness reads as high status; bowing and asymmetry read as deference or defiance.
groups.alternatives: Bowing is a normal greeting in many cultures and signals respect rather than low status; read status cues against the customs of the scene.
concepts: Part III — status and power in posture
groups.prompt_tip: State the status relationship in body terms: 'upright centered stance, hands behind back, commanding' or 'slight bow, hands together, deferential'.

lessons.title: Gestures and hands
lessons.objective: Show the communicative function of hands and culturally contextual gestures.
lessons.source_note: Danbooru gesture categories; cultural interpretations must be contextualized.
lessons.intro: Faces get most of the attention, but hands talk too. In this lesson TSMC keeps the same neutral face and full-body framing while her hands do all the communicating — greeting, offering, counting, asking for quiet. Some of these gestures feel universal, but many are learned emblems whose meaning depends on culture and context, so read them carefully.
lessons.exercise: Cover the captions and sort the fifteen gesture plates into two piles: gestures you think anyone anywhere would understand, and gestures that require cultural context. Then check your second pile against the emblematic group.
lessons.exercise_answer: The second pile should hold most of the emblems: bowing, palms together, the V sign and the thumbs-up all change meaning — or become meaningless or rude — across cultures. Even 'obvious' gestures like beckoning differ from place to place, so treat every emblem as local until you know the audience.

groups.title: Social gestures
groups.fixed: Same full-body framing and neutral face.
groups.learn: Learn that a single raised hand can run a whole social exchange — greeting, calling someone over, stopping them, offering help or apologizing — with the face staying neutral.
observe: Wave: one open hand raised in greeting; Beckon: fingers curling toward herself.
Stop: palm extended outward toward the viewer; Offer: open palm extended upward.
Apology: both hands joined near the chest with a slight inclination of the body.
groups.meaning: Everyday social gestures let characters manage an interaction — opening it, directing it, pausing it or repairing it — without any words.
groups.alternatives: The raised palm of Stop can also read as a greeting or a pledge, and a beckoning curl means 'go away' in some cultures, so the surrounding scene has to disambiguate.
concepts: Part II — gesture and line of action
groups.prompt_tip: Name the gesture and the hand shape explicitly, e.g. 'raising one open hand in a wave, palm facing outward', rather than just saying 'greeting someone'.

groups.title: Emblematic gestures
groups.fixed: Use the described gesture without asserting universal meaning.
groups.learn: Learn to recognize emblematic gestures — signs with dictionary-like meanings — and to notice that each meaning belongs to a culture, not to the human body in general.
observe: Thumbs up: thumb raised with the other fingers folded; Peace sign: index and middle fingers raised, palm outward.
Palms together: hands pressed together at the chest; Formal bow: upper torso inclined forward with arms relaxed.
Hand over heart: right palm placed over the chest.
groups.meaning: Emblems such as the thumbs up, the V sign, pressed palms and a bow deliver a complete, wordless message — approval, peace, thanks or respect — in a single pose.
groups.alternatives: None of these is universal: the V sign palm-inward is an insult in some countries, the thumbs up is rude in parts of the world, and pressed palms can signal prayer, greeting or apology depending on context.
concepts: Part III — symbols and cultural meaning (Lesson 15)
Part II — gesture and line of action
groups.prompt_tip: Name the emblem and its orientation precisely — 'V sign with the palm facing outward' — and add the intended meaning, because the same hand shape can carry opposite messages.

lessons.title: Action and implied motion
lessons.objective: Learn to depict verbs and stages of movement in still pictures.
lessons.source_note: Danbooru action vocabulary; curated motion studies.
lessons.intro: A still picture cannot move, yet it can clearly show an action. This lesson studies how a frozen pose implies a verb: what the body does just before, during and after a movement tells the viewer what is happening. The final group breaks one throw into its four phases, the same phases animators use to make motion believable.
lessons.exercise: Shuffle the four throw frames from Action phases out of order, then put them back in sequence. Point to the exact body details that tell you which frame is the preparation.
lessons.exercise_answer: Preparation is the frame with bent knees and the throwing arm drawn back while still holding the ball: the body coils before it acts. Release follows (arm extended), then follow-through (arm crossed, ball gone), then recovery (standing still, hands empty).

groups.title: Café verbs
groups.fixed: Same café furniture, camera and cup design; pose may change.
groups.learn: Learn that an action reads through the object being handled: the position of cup, teapot and spoon at one frozen moment is enough to name the verb.
observe: Sip: the cup is raised to her lips; Set down: the cup is being lowered onto its saucer.
Pour: a small teapot tilts over the cup; Stir: a spoon rotates inside the cup.
Spill: the cup tips and tea is visibly falling.
groups.meaning: Small, precise hand-and-object poses turn a still café scene into a sequence of recognizable everyday actions.
groups.alternatives: Mid-action poses can be ambiguous — a cup halfway to the lips could be raising or lowering — so the saucer, spoon and teapot positions matter as supporting evidence.
concepts: Part II — gesture and line of action
Part III — props and environmental storytelling (Lesson 14)
groups.prompt_tip: Describe the verb as a frozen moment with its object: 'tilting a small teapot over the cup, tea mid-pour', rather than asking for the action in general.

groups.title: Locomotion
groups.fixed: Same backdrop and full-body crop.
groups.learn: Learn how the whole body implies speed and balance: stride, lean and contact with the ground separate walking from running, jumping, falling and recovering.
observe: Walk: natural mid-stride pose with opposite arm swing; Run: forward lean with an airborne stride.
Jump: both feet off the floor with bent knees; Trip: balance lost, arms reaching out.
Recover: stance regained with one foot planted firmly.
groups.meaning: Locomotion is drawn through posture and ground contact — the less stable and more extended the body, the faster and riskier the movement feels.
groups.alternatives: A trip and a recover can look similar frame by frame; what separates them is the direction of the lean and whether a foot has found the ground, which is why the two plates belong side by side.
concepts: Part II — gesture and line of action
groups.prompt_tip: State the ground contact and lean explicitly — 'both feet off the ground, knees bent, mid-jump' or 'leaning forward, one foot planted, regaining balance'.

groups.title: Action phases
groups.fixed: Use an imaginary light ball; fixed camera and consistent floor.
groups.learn: Learn the four phases every believable action passes through — preparation, the action itself, follow-through and recovery — by reading them as a four-frame sequence of one throw.
observe: Anticipation: knees bent and the throwing arm drawn back, holding the ball.
Action: the throwing arm extends and releases the ball; Follow-through: the arm crosses the body as the ball leaves the frame.
Recovery: she settles back into a standing position with empty hands.
groups.meaning: Movement in still images is a before-and-after story: the drawn-back arm promises the throw, and the crossed arm and empty hands prove it happened.
groups.alternatives: Shown alone, the anticipation frame could be read as winding up for a punch or a dance move; only its place in the sequence fixes it as the start of a throw.
concepts: Part II — gesture and line of action
groups.prompt_tip: For an action sequence, prompt each phase separately with the same character, camera and setting, naming the phase: 'anticipation pose — knees bent, arm drawn back before the throw'.

lessons.title: Interpersonal relationships
lessons.objective: Show social relationships through coordinated behavior.
lessons.source_note: Danbooru interaction vocabulary; curated relationship studies.
lessons.intro: One character shows an emotion; two characters show a relationship. Here TSMC and her companion keep the same café table and chairs while their coordinated behavior changes — leaning in or folding arms, helping or excluding. The lesson is that relationships are drawn with pairs of bodies, not single expressions.
lessons.exercise: Without reading the captions, sort the Conflict group's plates into 'competing' and 'arguing'. What visual evidence separates rivalry from disagreement?
lessons.exercise_answer: Rivalry is competitive parallel focus: both women lean forward with the same intense effort, aimed at a shared goal. Disagreement is contradiction: one gestures openly while the other folds her arms, so the two bodies send opposite signals.

groups.title: Affiliation
groups.fixed: Same two identities, chairs and table; expressions and posture may change.
groups.learn: Learn that friendliness between two people is drawn as coordination: matching lean, shared focus and offered touch, not just two smiles at once.
observe: Friendship: both lean in toward each other with warm smiles.
Mentorship: TSMC points out a detail while her companion listens; Cooperation: both inspect a wafer together.
Support: TSMC offers a reassuring hand on her companion's shoulder.
groups.meaning: Affiliation shows in bodies angled toward each other and attention shared on the same thing — the pair behaves as one unit.
groups.alternatives: The same lean-in can read as romantic interest or as conspiring, depending on the story around it; coordinated posture signals closeness, not its exact kind.
concepts: Part II — eye path and gaze
groups.prompt_tip: Direct both characters, not one: 'both women lean in over the table, smiling at each other' works better than describing a single friendly pose.

groups.title: Conflict
groups.fixed: No violence or props beyond agreed café items.
groups.learn: Learn to tell kinds of conflict apart: rivalry is two people straining toward the same goal, disagreement is crossed signals, and reconciliation is the visible undoing of both.
observe: Rivalry: both lean forward competitively with focused gazes.
Disagreement: one gestures while the other folds her arms; Distrust: one guards her cup and watches the other sideways.
Reconciliation: both relax and reach toward a handshake.
groups.meaning: Conflict is drawn as mismatched or competing body language — parallel effort for rivalry, contradictory gesture and posture for disagreement.
groups.alternatives: Folded arms in Disagreement can also mean cold, tiredness or self-comfort; it reads as conflict here because the partner's open gesturing contradicts it.
concepts: Part II — gesture and line of action
groups.prompt_tip: Give each character an opposing instruction — 'one explains with open hands while the other sits back with folded arms' — so the tension is built into the pair.

lessons.title: Proxemics and blocking
lessons.objective: Explore distance, orientation, and shared attention.
lessons.source_note: Curated staging; distance norms vary by culture and context.
lessons.intro: Where people sit is a message. This lesson changes only the staging — how far apart the chairs are, which way the bodies face, and where the two gazes land — while expressions stay near neutral. Distance and orientation quietly tell the viewer how close, formal or disconnected a relationship is, though the exact norms differ across cultures.
lessons.exercise: Look at the Distance ladder with the expressions covered. Rank the three plates from most intimate to most formal, then say what social change you feel as the chairs move apart — and check whether you would draw the line at the same distance for two strangers in your own culture.
lessons.exercise_answer: As distance grows with expression held fixed, the scene shifts from closeness toward formality or estrangement: perceived intimacy is carried by spacing alone. But the thresholds are personal and cultural — avoid treating any universal distance as the rule, and note how much of your ranking came from your own norms.

groups.title: Distance
groups.fixed: Use a fixed wider crop with movable chairs and identical table.
groups.learn: Learn to read seating distance as a volume knob for intimacy: the same two people, table and neutral expressions feel like confidants, colleagues or strangers purely by how far apart the chairs sit.
observe: Close: the chairs and bodies are near each other without crowding.
Conversational: a normal seated distance across the table.
Distant: the chairs are pulled apart with clear empty space between them.
groups.meaning: Physical distance stands in for social distance — closer staging suggests trust and intimacy, wider staging suggests formality or estrangement.
groups.alternatives: Wide spacing can simply mean a big table, a formal venue or a culture with larger personal-space norms; distance suggests a relationship but never proves one, and there is no universal threshold in centimetres.
concepts: Part II — composition and spatial arrangement
groups.prompt_tip: Specify the chair spacing and the gap, e.g. 'the two chairs pulled far apart with empty floor visible between them', rather than relying on the word 'distant' alone.

groups.title: Orientation
groups.fixed: Keep both chairs at the same distance from each other.
groups.learn: Learn that which way bodies face is a second staging channel: orientation can connect two people, align them as a team, cut them off, or leave a conversation one-sided — all at the same distance.
observe: Face to face: the two torsos directly face each other; Side by side: both face the same direction.
Back to back: both are turned away from each other.
Unequal orientation: TSMC faces her partner while the partner turns aside.
groups.meaning: Orientation shows whether attention is exchanged, shared toward something else, refused, or offered and not returned.
groups.alternatives: Side-by-side seating can mean intimacy (watching a sunset together) or avoidance (refusing to face each other); what they are both facing decides which reading wins.
concepts: Part II — composition and spatial arrangement

groups.title: Attention triangle
groups.fixed: Same wafer on tabletop and same seating.
groups.learn: Learn to trace the attention triangle: two faces and one object. Where the two gazes land — on each other, on the wafer, split, or nowhere — tells you whether the pair is connecting, collaborating, mismatched or checked out.
observe: Mutual gaze: both look at each other; Joint attention: both look at the wafer on the table.
One-sided attention: TSMC looks at her companion, who looks at the wafer.
Disengagement: both look away in opposite directions.
groups.meaning: Shared attention is the smallest unit of a relationship in a picture: looking at the same thing together is what turns two figures into a pair.
groups.alternatives: A split gaze can also mean one person is presenting the object to the other — a teaching moment rather than a mismatch — so hands and posture have to confirm the colder reading.
concepts: Part II — implied line and gaze
groups.prompt_tip: Give each character an explicit gaze target — 'both look down at the wafer between them' or 'she watches her companion, who stares at the wafer' — since gaze direction is the whole cue.

lessons.title: Subtext and contradiction
lessons.objective: Distinguish visible behavior from implied private intention.
lessons.source_note: Curated acting and visual-narrative examples.
lessons.intro: People rarely say exactly what they feel, and a picture can show that gap. In this lesson the words, the smile and the situations stay almost the same while the hidden intention changes — you learn to separate what a character is visibly doing from what they privately mean.
lessons.exercise: Read the words “Thank you.” under each of the four plates in group l11-g01, and say aloud how each delivery would sound.
lessons.exercise_answer: The words never change, but they can imply sincerity (relaxed smile, open hands), reluctance (tight polite smile, rigid shoulders), sarcasm (one-sided smile, skeptical brows) or discomfort (averted gaze, hesitant hands) — the body supplies the tone.

groups.title: Same words different delivery
groups.fixed: The page supplies identical dialogue: Thank you. Do not render lettering.
groups.learn: The same two words — “Thank you.” — sit under all four plates, yet each plate means something different. Delivery, not wording, carries the real message: face, hands and shoulders tell you whether the thanks are sincere, forced, sarcastic or awkward.
observe: The relaxed smile and open hands in the sincere plate, against the tight polite smile and rigid shoulders in the reluctant plate
The one-sided smile and skeptical brows that turn the third plate sarcastic
The averted gaze and hesitant hand movement in the awkward plate
groups.meaning: Identical words can express sincere gratitude, reluctant politeness, sarcasm or embarrassment depending on how the body delivers them.
groups.alternatives: A tight smile could also be read as shyness or tiredness rather than reluctance, and norms for eye contact and smiling vary across cultures — posture and context together narrow the reading.
concepts: Part II — body language and posture
groups.prompt_tip: Prompt the delivery, not the dialogue: write “a tight polite smile with rigid shoulders” rather than asking the model to render the words “thank you”.

lessons.title: Manga visual vocabulary
lessons.objective: Learn conventional drawn signs, separate from realistic acting.
lessons.source_note: Cohn and Ehly manga morphology inspired; original illustrations.
lessons.intro: Manga and comics add a second channel on top of realistic acting: small drawn signs — a sweat drop, a burst of rays, a trail of speed lines — that state a feeling or a movement directly. This lesson separates that graphic vocabulary from the character's actual expression, so you can see what each channel contributes.
lessons.exercise: Pick any plate in Lesson 12 and cover its graphic sign with your thumb. How much of the meaning survives?
lessons.exercise_answer: The face and pose keep their realistic expression, but the specific named state — confusion, dizziness, a new idea — disappears. Realistic expression and conventional manga marks are separate channels, and the full reading is the two added together.

groups.title: Emotion signs
groups.fixed: Keep base facial pixels if possible; add only the visual sign.
groups.learn: Six plates keep the same portrait and add one conventional emotion sign each. These marks are a shared code between artist and reader: you learn them the way you learn words, and once learned they read instantly.
observe: The single large sweat drop beside the temple and the small cross-shaped anger vein above the brow
The short diagonal blush hatching on the cheeks and the vertical gloom lines above the forehead
The small star-shaped sparkles around the face and the floating question mark above the head
groups.meaning: A small graphic symbol can name an emotion — embarrassment, anger, gloom, admiration, confusion — without changing the face at all.
groups.alternatives: These signs are conventions of Japanese manga and anime; a reader unfamiliar with them may take the sweat drop literally as heat or effort, and other comics traditions use different marks for the same feelings.
groups.prompt_tip: Name the sign and its placement: “a single large manga sweat drop beside her temple, anime style” — image models know most of these marks by name.

groups.title: Cognitive and physical signs
groups.fixed: Use original graphic marks; no speech bubbles.
groups.learn: This group covers signs for thoughts and body states rather than emotions: ideas, sleep, dizziness, shock, a sigh and a trailing pause. They let a still image show invisible mental events.
observe: The small glowing light bulb above the head and the translucent sleep bubble at the nose
The small stars orbiting the head and the short radiating shock rays around it
The small breath cloud at the mouth and the three dots of the ellipsis near the head
groups.meaning: Graphic signs can externalize thinking and physical sensation, turning “she just had an idea” or “she is dizzy” into something visible.
groups.alternatives: Some of these marks come from a wider cartoon tradition — the light bulb is common in Western comics too — while the nose sleep bubble is specific to manga and may puzzle readers who expect “Zzz” instead.
groups.prompt_tip: Describe the mark plainly and keep it small: “three small dots trailing beside her head, manga ellipsis, no speech bubble”.

groups.title: Motion signs
groups.fixed: Use fixed action pose derived from lesson 8; vary only graphic marks.
groups.learn: The action pose from Lesson 8 stays fixed in this group; only the drawn marks change. Motion in comics is rarely carried by the body alone — lines and bursts tell you speed, path, impact and emphasis.
observe: The parallel speed lines behind the moving body and the curved motion arcs beside the arm
The jagged impact burst where the foot lands and the faint repeated silhouette of the afterimage
The short wavy tremble marks beside the arms and the converging focus rays on the held object
groups.meaning: Different marks encode different physics: speed, trajectory, impact, trembling and attention can each be drawn with a dedicated sign.
groups.alternatives: Speed lines and focus rays also appear in Western comics and advertising, but their density and placement follow manga conventions; without the marks, the same pose could read as a static stance.
concepts: Part III — motion in still images
groups.prompt_tip: Specify the mark type and what it attaches to: “parallel speed lines trailing behind her moving body” or “a jagged impact burst where her foot lands”.

lessons.title: Atmosphere and emotional context
lessons.objective: See how story cues change mood even under fixed light and color.
lessons.source_note: Curated mood studies; Part 2 owns lighting recipes.
lessons.intro: Mood is not made by light and color alone — the Seeing course covered those tools. Here the daylight and the camera never change; only the story evidence inside the café changes, and the same seat becomes cozy, lonely, uneasy or absurd.
lessons.exercise: Compare the lonely and cozy plates in group l13-g01. The light is identical — list everything else that differs.
lessons.exercise_answer: Props, unused seating, gaze and action can change mood independently of lighting: an open book and a fresh pastry with a relaxed pose feel cozy, while an unused second cup and a distant gaze make the same café, in the same daylight, feel lonely.

groups.title: Café atmosphere
groups.fixed: Keep original daylight and camera; vary story evidence only.
groups.learn: Six plates share one café, one camera and one daylight, yet each has a different emotional temperature. Small story details — a pastry, an envelope, an old photograph — steer the mood more than the setting does.
observe: The open book and fresh pastry in the cozy plate, against the unused second cup and distant gaze in the lonely plate
The unopened envelope and guarded gaze in the uneasy plate
The old photograph near the cup in the nostalgic plate, the untouched cup facing an empty seat in the expectant plate, and the tiny toy crown balanced on the cup in the absurd plate
groups.meaning: Atmosphere is built from narrative clues: what is on the table and where her attention sits decide whether the same room feels warm, empty or strange.
groups.alternatives: The tiny crown could be read as playful or celebratory rather than absurd, and an unopened envelope might signal happy anticipation instead of unease — mood readings lean on the viewer's own expectations.
concepts: Part III — props and set dressing
groups.prompt_tip: Prompt mood through objects and attention, not adjectives: “an untouched second cup across from her, her gaze distant” makes loneliness visible.

lessons.title: Props and environmental storytelling
lessons.objective: Use objects and traces to imply events without showing them.
lessons.source_note: Iconclass and Visual Genome inspired; original scenes.
lessons.intro: Stories leave evidence behind. This lesson shows how a single object on a table, or the traces people leave in a room, can imply a whole event that the picture never shows directly — the viewer reconstructs what happened from what remains.
lessons.exercise: Choose any plate in group l14-g02 and, before reading its label, write down the event you think just happened.
lessons.exercise_answer: Object traces suggest a plausible event, not a unique fact: a pulled-out chair and a steaming cup strongly imply a recent departure, but the reconstruction is your inference — a different viewer can build a different story from the same traces.

groups.title: One changed prop
groups.fixed: Cup, pose, camera, light and furniture fixed; change tabletop clue.
groups.learn: Everything in the café stays fixed except one object on the table — and each object starts a different story in the viewer's head. A prop is a compressed plot: it implies a before and an after.
observe: The sealed envelope and the stopped, cracked wristwatch
The small trophy and the single wilted flower
The single unfamiliar key and the two unlettered admission tickets
groups.meaning: One well-chosen object can imply an event, a relationship or a decision — a sealed letter suggests news waiting, a broken watch suggests lost time, two tickets suggest a companion expected.
groups.alternatives: Props are read through cultural habits: two tickets might mean a date, a gift or a refund, and a key might be hers rather than a stranger's — the picture suggests a story but does not settle it.
concepts: Part III — props and set dressing
groups.prompt_tip: Add one story-bearing object and keep everything else plain: “a single unfamiliar key on the table beside her cup” — extra props dilute the implication.

groups.title: Evidence of past events
groups.fixed: Do not change daylight or camera; use environmental traces.
groups.learn: Nobody performs an action in these plates; the room itself tells what just happened. Spills, steam, crumbs and displaced furniture are traces, and the viewer reconstructs the event from its aftermath.

lessons.title: Symbols and cultural meaning
lessons.objective: Learn conventional, contextual and invented symbols without claiming universality.
lessons.source_note: Iconclass and Chinese Iconography Thesaurus inspired; verify cultural notes separately.
lessons.intro: Symbols are pictures with agreed meanings: an object stands for an idea you cannot photograph, like fairness or passing time. This lesson separates three kinds of symbols — widely shared conventions, meanings that belong to a particular culture, and symbols invented for this series — because a symbol only works when its audience has learned it.
lessons.exercise: Pick one symbol from this lesson — the lotus, the peach or the wafer halo — and describe two different interpretations it could carry.
lessons.exercise_answer: There is no single correct pair: the point is that meaning depends on cultural tradition and context. A peach is longevity in Chinese iconography but just fruit elsewhere; a wafer halo only means power to viewers the series has taught. Credit any answer that names the tradition or context behind each reading.

groups.title: Objects as symbols
groups.fixed: Same character posture and simple stage; one symbolic object.
groups.learn: Some objects carry meanings so widely taught that viewers read them instantly: an hourglass means time, scales mean fairness. Learn to spot these conventional symbols — and to remember that even they are agreements a culture teaches, not facts built into the object.
observe: An hourglass, balanced scales, a key beside a closed box, a mirror — one familiar object per plate, held or faced on the same plain stage.
The seedling and the two separated chain links trade on resemblance: growing and breaking are visible in the object itself.
Her pose, costume and the empty stage stay the same in every plate, so the object is the only thing that changes.
groups.meaning: A single familiar object can stand for an abstract idea — time, fairness, access, reflection, freedom, growth — without any words.
groups.alternatives: A key can also promise secrecy or warn of being locked out, and a mirror can suggest vanity rather than reflection; context, not the object alone, settles the reading.
concepts: Part III — Lesson 14: props as evidence
groups.prompt_tip: Name the object and the idea together — 'holding balanced scales to suggest fairness' — rather than asking for the abstract word alone.

groups.title: Cultural contextual examples
groups.fixed: Keep costume canonical; add object, not a new historical style.
groups.learn: Many symbols belong to a tradition: the peach means long life in Chinese iconography, and marigolds mean remembrance in Mexico's Día de Muertos. Learn to ask whose symbol it is before using it, because the same object can be festive in one culture and funereal in another.
observe: A lotus, a paper crane and a peach — three East Asian motifs of purity, awakening and longevity.
An olive branch and a white dove, the Mediterranean pair long associated with peace.
Orange marigolds, the flower laid out for the dead in Día de Muertos observance.
groups.meaning: These objects carry their meanings inside specific cultural traditions — Buddhist art, Chinese iconography, Mediterranean custom, Mexican remembrance — not everywhere at once.
groups.alternatives: Outside its tradition, a marigold is just a cheerful garden flower and a crane just a bird; viewers who have not learned the code will read the object literally.
concepts: Part I — ukiyo-e and East Asian print traditions

groups.title: Invented Silicon Wars symbols
groups.fixed: Do not add words or logos beyond canon.
groups.learn: A series can mint its own symbols: repeat an invented image with a fixed meaning and the audience learns it, the way readers learn any convention. These four plates propose a private code for the Silicon Wars world — power, fragility, interdependence, absence — built from wafers, dies and cleanroom gear.
observe: A circular wafer floats behind her head exactly where a halo would sit in an altarpiece.
A cracked chip die is held carefully in both hands; two other chips are locked edge to edge.
An empty cleanroom glove dangles from her hand, shaped by the hand that is not in it.
groups.meaning: Invented symbols can carry precise meanings — technological power, fragility, interdependence, absence — once a story teaches them by repetition.
groups.alternatives: A first-time viewer may read the wafer halo as a hat or a rising sun; invented symbols fail silently until the work has taught them.
concepts: Part I — religious iconography and the halo

lessons.title: Visual rhetoric and metaphor
lessons.objective: Communicate abstract claims through visual relationships.
lessons.source_note: VisMet and MetaCLUE inspired; original metaphors.
lessons.intro: A metaphor says one thing is another: a supply chain becomes a row of dominoes, an industry becomes a garden. These plates use impossible objects and deliberate exaggerations to make abstract claims — about time, fragility and dependence — visible at a glance. Each construction is a small argument, and each can be argued with.
lessons.exercise: Of the four dependency metaphors — bridge, foundation, network, dominoes — which one best conveys fragility? Defend your choice.
lessons.exercise_answer: Dominoes and foundation usually foreground fragility best: dominoes promise a cascade from one small failure, and a foundation concentrates all risk in a single supporting piece. Bridge stresses the load carried across and network stresses connection, so answers choosing them should explain which facet of fragility they highlight.

groups.title: Metaphorical constructions
groups.fixed: Same neutral rendering; permit impossible objects.
groups.learn: Metaphors are built, not found: put two things together (juxtaposition), melt them into one object (fusion), swap a part (replacement), give a thing a body (personification), or blow the scale up or down (hyperbole, understatement). Learn the six constructions and you can take any metaphor apart.
observe: A giant hourglass is filled with microchips instead of sand; a ceramic cup merges halfway into an integrated circuit.
A tiny wafer sits where a clock's missing gear should be, and a small chip pleads with a humanlike posture.
Scale does the talking twice: a colossal wafer balanced on one finger, then one tiny chip alone on an otherwise empty table.
groups.meaning: Abstract claims about time, dependence and importance become visible when two objects are combined, swapped or rescaled.
groups.alternatives: The pleading chip can read as cute rather than serious, and the giant hourglass as a surreal joke; tone decides whether a metaphor persuades or entertains.
groups.prompt_tip: Name the construction, not just the idea: 'a ceramic cup fused halfway into an integrated circuit' gives the generator a buildable object.

groups.title: Rhetorical intentions
groups.fixed: Illustrate concept; page explains alternative readings.
groups.learn: Pictures can argue. Allegory sustains one comparison across a whole scene, irony shows care lavished on something already broken, paradox builds an impossible fit, satire exaggerates a target's vanity, a visual pun swaps part of a word for a picture, and contrast lets two held objects state the claim. Learn to name the intention behind the device.
observe: She tends a garden of chip seedlings; she carefully polishes a trophy that is visibly cracked.
An oversized key cannot enter its tiny matching lock; a tower of empty ceremonial awards blocks a workbench.
A ceramic cup has a literal silicon chip missing from its rim, and her two hands hold a fragile wafer and a sturdy stone.
groups.meaning: Each plate makes a claim — about an industry, an honour, a mismatch — by choosing a rhetorical device, not by stating the claim in words.
groups.alternatives: Satire is the easiest to misread: a viewer who misses the target may take the tower of awards as sincere celebration, which is why satire needs a recognisable target.
groups.prompt_tip: Prompt the device and its target together — 'carefully polishing a visibly cracked trophy, irony' — so the contradiction, not just the object, survives generation.

groups.title: One idea multiple metaphors
groups.fixed: Target dependency in every image.
groups.learn: One abstract idea — dependency, the fact that everything rests on something else — can be pictured as a bridge, a foundation, a network or a row of dominoes. Learn to compare metaphors for the same idea: each highlights a different facet, and each quietly hides the others.
observe: She physically supports a bridge that carries miniature chips across.
A single wafer bears a whole tower of chips; she holds the central knot of a web connecting chips.
A line of precariously balanced chips leans on one foundational chip at its base.
groups.meaning: Dependency can be pictured as support from below, connection through a centre, or a load carried across — same claim, different emphasis.
groups.alternatives: The network version can read as control rather than dependence — she holds the knot, so she may look like the one in charge; who holds the structure changes the claim.
concepts: Part III — Lesson 14: props and traces
groups.prompt_tip: When an idea matters, prompt two or three metaphors for it — 'dependency as a foundation' versus 'dependency as dominoes' — and choose the facet you actually mean.

lessons.title: Narrative moments
lessons.objective: Recognize the role a single picture plays within an event.
lessons.source_note: Cohn visual narrative grammar inspired; terms adapted pedagogically.
lessons.intro: A story is a chain of moments, and every picture in the chain has a job: setting the scene, starting the trouble, paying it off. This lesson freezes the beats of two small events so you can name what each single frame contributes. The frames work together; no single frame isolates one variable.
lessons.exercise: Look at the four 'Before or after' frames and select the one frame that most strongly implies a prior event. What is your evidence?
lessons.exercise_answer: The strongest answers usually pick the empty room: compare the visible evidence — the closed door, the empty chair, the second cup left behind — with what the audience must infer, namely that a meeting happened and ended. The untouched cup in the 'before' frame implies the future instead, which is the useful contrast.

groups.title: The mysterious envelope
groups.fixed: Same envelope, room, costume and fixed wide camera.
groups.learn: A complete mini-story can be told in eight stills if each frame does one job: establish, trigger, anticipation, discovery, reaction, decision, resolution, aftermath. Learn the beat names so you can plan a sequence — and notice that cause and effect live in the order, not in any single frame.
observe: The same sealed envelope, room, costume and fixed wide camera appear in every frame; only her actions change.
The middle beats slow down: she turns toward the envelope, reaches toward the seal without opening it, and only then opens it to find a small wafer.
The story closes the loop — the wafer is placed safely in a box, and the final frame leaves her sitting quietly beside the closed box.
groups.meaning: Ordered beats turn a simple event — opening a letter — into a story with suspense, a turn and a settling end.

groups.title: Before or after
groups.fixed: Same props and camera; each image is a distinct instant.
groups.learn: A single picture can point backward or forward in time. An untouched cup says 'not yet'; an empty chair and a second cup say 'already over'. Learn to read these time clues — including the boldest one, a frame with nobody in it at all.
observe: Before arrival: an empty seat and an untouched cup while she waits; at the arrival, she notices her companion entering the doorway.
After departure, the room stands empty: door closed, chair empty, a second cup left on the table and her mask left behind on it.
The last frame refuses closure — she pauses at the closed door, still holding the sealed envelope.
groups.meaning: Props and absences let one frame imply what happened just before it, or what is about to happen next.
groups.alternatives: The empty room could be read as 'before anyone arrived' rather than 'after they left'; the second cup is the detail that tips it toward after.

lessons.title: Sequential visual grammar
lessons.objective: Learn how panel selection and order create inference.
lessons.source_note: Cohn visual narrative grammar; curated continuity exercises.
lessons.intro: Comics and film tell stories by choosing which moments to show and which to skip. Read in order, these short sequences show how readers fill the gaps — inferring causes, elapsed time and even a second storyline running in parallel. Order is the grammar: shuffle the frames and the story changes.
lessons.exercise: In the 'Ellipsis and inference' sequence, remove the middle panel — the doorway frame — and explain what can still be inferred from the two remaining frames.
lessons.exercise_answer: Almost everything essential survives: ellipsis works when the preceding and subsequent states supply the evidence. Sealed envelope inside the café, then open empty envelope and a relieved face, lets readers infer the trip out and the delivery without ever seeing the doorway crossed.

groups.title: Cup accident
groups.fixed: Fixed camera and identical cup; no lettering.
groups.learn: The classic four-beat sequence — establisher, initial, peak, release — is the skeleton of visual narrative grammar. The peak, the falling cup, only reads as an accident because the establisher showed the cup safe at the table's edge and the release shows the cost.
observe: Frame one plants the cause: the cup rests near the edge of the table while she reads, absorbed.
Her elbow nudges the cup; then the cup falls and the tea arcs down — the peak is the one frame that could not be still.
The release lands on consequences: spilled tea, the intact cup on the floor, and her looking at the result.
groups.meaning: Cause, climax and consequence, dealt out one frame at a time, let readers reconstruct an event they never saw whole.
groups.alternatives: Without the first frame, the falling cup could be a deliberate throw; the establisher is what makes it an accident rather than an act.
concepts: Part I — comics and the gutter
groups.prompt_tip: Keep the camera and props identical across frames and vary only the action phase — 'cup at the table edge', 'cup falling, tea arcing down' — so the sequence reads as one event.

groups.title: The discovery
groups.fixed: Fixed camera and same envelope.
groups.learn: The same four-beat skeleton carries a happier event: an envelope opened, a wafer lifted out, a smile, the prize stored safely. Learn that the grammar is neutral — establisher, initial, peak and release describe the shape of an event, whatever its emotion.
observe: She faces the sealed envelope on the table; she opens it — the first two frames differ in the envelope's state.
The peak is a reveal: she lifts an iridescent wafer out of the envelope.
The release resolves into care: smiling, she sets the wafer into its protective case.
groups.meaning: A discovery follows the same narrative grammar as an accident; structure and feeling are separate choices.
groups.alternatives: The lifted wafer could be a peak of alarm instead of delight if the final frame showed alarm; the release frame is what fixes the event's emotional sign.
groups.prompt_tip: Prompt the emotional sign in the final frame — 'smiling as she sets it into its case' — because the release frame tells readers how to feel about the peak.

groups.title: Parallel actions
groups.fixed: Same two characters and props; preserve screen positions.
groups.learn: Stories can run two threads at once. The A and B labels mark alternating attention: her thread — writing a note, then sending it — and her companion's thread — examining a chip, then noticing the note. Learn how cutting between two simultaneous actions builds one shared event.
observe: She writes a note while her companion looks away; the companion then examines a small chip while she writes.
She pushes the folded note toward her companion, who notices it and reaches for it — the two threads meet.
Both characters keep their screen positions in every frame, so the cuts never confuse who is who.
groups.meaning: Alternating between two simultaneous actions lets a sequence show cause in one thread and effect in the other.
groups.alternatives: Read in isolation, the chip-examining frame could belong to a different story entirely; the note crossing the table is the stitch that joins the threads.
concepts: Part II — eye path and screen direction
groups.prompt_tip: Fix each character's screen position in every prompt — 'TSMC left, companion right' — and change only who acts, so parallel cuts stay readable.

groups.title: Ellipsis and inference
groups.fixed: Same doorway and envelope; middle panel optional on page.
groups.learn: Ellipsis is the art of leaving a frame out. Here the middle frame — stepping through the doorway — is the one the page lets you hide, because the before and after frames supply the evidence: a sealed envelope in hand, then an open, empty one and a relieved face. Learn what readers can rebuild from endpoints alone.
observe: Before: she stands inside the café holding the sealed envelope.
Transition: she steps through the doorway with the envelope — the frame the exercise removes.
After: she returns with the envelope open and empty, her expression relieved.
groups.meaning: When the states before and after are clear, the audience happily supplies the missing middle.
groups.alternatives: The relieved return could hide a delivery, a refusal or a loss; ellipsis guarantees that an event happened, not which event it was.

groups.title: Reaction cut
groups.fixed: Camera may cut between approved eye-line matched medium shots.

observe: Her companion reveals a cracked wafer — the stimulus is given its own frame.

groups.alternatives: Her restrained shock could be read as professional assessment rather than dismay; the careful reach in the third frame is what confirms concern.
concepts: Part I — film stills and editing

lessons.title: Genre and narrative framing
lessons.objective: Use the same premise to create different genre expectations without changing art style.
lessons.source_note: Curated narrative genres; no copying specific films.
lessons.intro: Genre is a promise about what kind of story you are in, and the promise is made with clues, not with drawing style. This lesson keeps the neutral digital painting and the daylight fixed and changes only plot cues — props, events, and stakes — so the same envelope scene can become a mystery, a comedy, a science fiction story, a fantasy, a drama, or a suspense scene. If the genre changes while the rendering does not, the genre must be living in the story elements.
lessons.exercise: Keep the style constant. Which clues signal genre?
lessons.exercise_answer: Look for plot cues, objects, and stakes rather than a new visual style: an unfamiliar key promises mystery, a comically oversized receipt promises comedy, a tiny holographic circuit promises science fiction. The rendering — neutral digital painting in daylight — never changes, so anything that tells you the genre must be something the story is doing, not something the drawing is doing.

groups.title: One envelope six genres
groups.fixed: Keep neutral digital painting and daylight; change plot cues, not rendering.
groups.learn: Genre can be signaled by a single plot cue — an object, an event, or a stake — while the drawing style, lighting, and setting stay exactly the same. Each plate changes only what the envelope delivers, and that one change rewrites what kind of story you expect.
observe: The rendering never changes: same neutral digital painting, same daylight, same café staging in all six plates.

Each genre is carried by one prop or event: an unfamiliar key (mystery), a comically oversized receipt (comedy), a tiny holographic circuit (science fiction), a small luminous seedling (fantasy), a torn personal photograph (drama), a second envelope sliding under the closed door (suspense).
Her hesitation in the suspense plate and the personal, damaged photograph in the drama plate raise the stakes without any change of style.
groups.meaning: One premise — an envelope opened in a café — can promise six different genres, and the promise is made by plot cues alone.
groups.alternatives: Some cues cross genres: the glowing seedling could read as science fiction rather than fantasy, and the unfamiliar key could open a thriller instead of a mystery — genre readings depend on the stories a viewer already knows.
groups.prompt_tip: Name the genre and give one concrete plot prop or event — 'a sealed envelope containing an unfamiliar key, mystery mood' — instead of asking for a genre 'style'.

groups.title: Archetypal roles
groups.fixed: Same outfit, camera and style; demonstrate role through action and prop.
groups.learn: A character's role can be read from what she does and what she handles, not from a costume change. Outfit, camera, and stage stay fixed; each role is demonstrated through one action and one prop.
observe: Mentor: she guides a small apprentice's hand toward a wafer. Guardian: she shields a fragile wafer with both hands.
Explorer: she studies an unfamiliar map and points ahead. Creator: she assembles a tiny circuit sculpture.
Trickster: she reveals a harmless hidden toy behind the cup. Ruler: she coordinates symbolic chip pieces arranged on a tabletop.
groups.meaning: Archetypal roles — mentor, guardian, explorer, creator, trickster, ruler — are communicated by action and by a character's relationship to objects, not by dress.
groups.alternatives: The Ruler's arranged chip pieces could also read as a strategist or a board-game player, and the Guardian's protective hands could read as a craftsperson simply being careful — context decides how far an archetype stretches.
groups.prompt_tip: Describe the role as an action with a prop — 'she guides a child's hand toward a delicate object, protective and patient' — rather than naming the archetype alone.

lessons.title: Integration and visual critique
lessons.objective: Practice communicating an intention and diagnosing why images fail.
lessons.source_note: Original capstone; some cards deliberately vary multiple variables.
lessons.intro: The capstone turns the whole course around: instead of reading a picture someone else made, you set a brief — one intended meaning — and judge how well each image delivers it. Some plates here are deliberately ambiguous or contradictory, included as teaching material so you can practice diagnosing why an image fails and how you would fix it. Treating a failed image as evidence, not embarrassment, is the working habit this lesson is for.
lessons.exercise: Explain why the unclear reconciliation image fails, then propose a revision.
lessons.exercise_answer: In the ambiguous plate there is no reciprocal gesture or posture — the two figures simply sit near each other without interacting — so the brief never lands. To revise it, strengthen shared attention and hand movement: have both figures turn toward each other, meet each other's gaze, and reach for the handshake together, as the clear plate does.

groups.title: Same visual brief three approaches
groups.fixed: Target anticipation; each solution changes a different channel.
groups.learn: One brief — show anticipation — can be solved through three different channels: the face, the body, or a prop. Comparing the three shows that meaning does not have to live in the face, and that a picture-maker can choose which channel carries it.
observe: Face only: subtly raised brows as she watches the cup, while body and props stay neutral.
Body only: she leans toward the entrance with a neutral face — the anticipation is in the lean.
Prop only: a sealed invitation beside the cup, with pose and expression kept neutral — the object supplies the expectation.
groups.meaning: Anticipation can be built from expression, from posture, or from a meaningful object; the skill is picking the channel deliberately.
groups.alternatives: The raised brows alone could be read as mild surprise or curiosity, and the sealed invitation could suggest a secret rather than anticipation — each single channel is weaker and more ambiguous than all three combined.
concepts: Part III — intended vs perceived meaning

groups.title: Clear versus unclear
groups.fixed: Target reconciliation; deliberately produce an instructive failure.
groups.learn: This group teaches by failure on purpose. The brief is reconciliation: one plate delivers it clearly, one is ambiguous, and one contradicts itself — and learning to say why the weak plates fail is the skill the whole course has been building toward.
observe: Clear: both women relax and reach toward a handshake — the gesture is mutual.
Ambiguous: both sit neutrally without any interaction; nothing in the frame answers the brief.
Contradictory: one reaches toward a handshake while the other turns away with tense shoulders — the two bodies tell opposite stories.
groups.meaning: Reconciliation reads clearly only when both figures reciprocate; a one-sided or absent gesture leaves the meaning undecided or reversed.
groups.alternatives: The ambiguous plate could be read as a calm pause before talks begin, and the contradictory plate as one character forgiving while the other is not yet ready — plausible stories, but neither is the brief that was asked for.
concepts: Part III — intended vs perceived meaning
groups.prompt_tip: For a two-person meaning, specify both sides of the exchange — 'both relax and reach for a handshake' — because a generator left to improvise often gives you only one.

groups.title: Final story
groups.fixed: Same café and fixed screen direction; multi-variable capstone.
groups.learn: The four frames assemble everything from the course — props, an arrival, a decision, an expression — into one short story told in sequence. Each frame changes several things at once, which is how real storytelling works once the single-variable training wheels come off.
observe: Setup: TSMC waits with a sealed envelope and an untouched cup. Complication: her companion arrives carrying a cracked wafer.
Decision: she opens the envelope and reveals a replacement wafer inside.
Resolution: the two exchange the wafer and smile with relief — the problem the sequence set up is closed.
groups.meaning: A complete miniature story — wait, problem, decision, relief — can be told in four still frames when each frame carries one beat.
groups.alternatives: Read alone, the final frame could be any friendly exchange; it means 'resolution' only because of the cracked wafer two frames earlier — sequence meaning is cumulative, and reordering the frames breaks the story.
concepts: Part III — sequence and narrative grammar
groups.prompt_tip: Brief a sequence beat by beat — 'frame 2: the companion arrives carrying the damaged object' — and keep screen direction and props consistent across frames.

lessons.title: Semantic experiment A — Same meaning, different implementation
lessons.objective: Show that one intended meaning can be built from many different visual mechanisms.
lessons.source_note: Supplementary semantic experiments (2026-11-26); mechanisms cross-reference Part II.
lessons.intro: Every earlier lesson changed one variable at a time; this experiment does the opposite. The meaning stays fixed — loneliness, authority, suspense, hope, vulnerability — and each group builds that one meaning four different ways, from four different bundles of visual mechanisms. These are recipes, not single-variable tests, and part of the lesson is judging which recipe convinces you, and being able to say why.
lessons.exercise: Pick one meaning and rank its four implementations from most to least convincing; name the mechanism that does the work in your favorite.
lessons.exercise_answer: There is no single correct ranking — the experiment is built so that reasonable viewers disagree. Strong answers name the mechanism rather than just the feeling: 'the empty place setting convinces me most, because the absence does the work' is an argument, while 'this one feels loneliest' is only a verdict.

groups.title: Loneliness, four ways
groups.fixed: The intended meaning (loneliness) stays fixed; the visual mechanism changes.
groups.learn: Loneliness is the fixed meaning here; what changes is the mechanism. Space, company, an unused place setting, and a companion's failed connection each produce the feeling by a different route — compare which one works on you, and why.
observe: Alone in space: she sits alone at a small table in a large, otherwise empty café, with much empty seating around her. Isolation in company: soft background silhouettes socialize while she sits apart.
The empty place: an unused opposite setting at her table implies someone who is not there.
The disconnected smile: a companion leans in toward her while she subtly withdraws — company that does not connect.
groups.meaning: Loneliness can be built from emptiness, from exclusion, from absence, or from failed contact — four mechanisms, one feeling.
groups.alternatives: The alone-in-space plate could read as peaceful solitude rather than loneliness — the same emptiness is restful or desolate depending on the viewer's own experience, which is why this experiment asks for your ranking rather than a correct answer.
concepts: Part III — absence and the empty place
Part III — intended vs perceived meaning
groups.prompt_tip: Pick the mechanism, not just the mood: 'she sits apart while blurred figures socialize behind her' builds a specific loneliness that 'she looks lonely' cannot.

groups.title: Authority, four ways
groups.fixed: The intended meaning (authority) stays fixed; the visual mechanism changes.
groups.learn: Authority is the fixed meaning; the mechanisms are camera height, posture, other people's attention, and formal symmetry. Notice that only one of the four works through the camera — the rest work through the body and through how other people behave around her.
observe: Low camera angle: the camera sits just below her eye line, so she stands tall over the viewer — a gentle low angle, not an extreme worm's-eye shot.
Posture: an upright torso with shoulders relaxed back. Others attend: she gives calm instructions while her companion attends.
Symmetry and setting: she is centered in a formal symmetrical composition against a plain ceremonial backdrop, chin level, hands clasped.
groups.meaning: Authority can come from how she is photographed, how she holds herself, how others respond to her, or how formally the scene is arranged.
groups.alternatives: The same cues can tip into arrogance or intimidation — a level chin and a steady gaze read as authority to some viewers and as coldness to others, and formality itself carries different weight in different cultures.
groups.prompt_tip: Name the authority mechanism you want — 'centered, symmetrical composition, chin level, hands clasped' — instead of the vague instruction 'make her look powerful'.

groups.title: Suspense, four ways
groups.fixed: The intended meaning (suspense) stays fixed; the visual mechanism changes.
groups.learn: Suspense is the fixed meaning, and none of the four plates shows a threat directly. Each one withholds something — an unopened envelope, an unseen entrance, an unexplained shadow, another person's alarm — and the withholding is what creates the tension.
observe: The unopened envelope: the envelope stays unopened under a guarded gaze. The off-frame look: her eyes go toward the café entrance, outside the frame.
The shadow at the door: a long unexplained human shadow falls across the floor from the closed door while she looks toward it, cup paused.
The companion's reaction: ASML reacts with startled alarm to something outside the frame while TSMC remains calm and looks at ASML — you read the danger in someone else's face.
groups.meaning: Suspense is built by pointing at what the viewer cannot see or cannot yet know.
groups.alternatives: The shadow could turn out to be a friend arriving, and the off-frame look mere curiosity — suspense lives in the gap before the explanation, and the same plates would read as calm if the story resolved them kindly.
groups.prompt_tip: Ask for the withholding, not the threat: 'an unexplained shadow falls from the closed door; she pauses and looks toward it' creates suspense that a visible monster would destroy.
