groups.title: Hope, four ways
groups.fixed: The intended meaning (hope) stays fixed; the visual mechanism changes.
groups.learn: Hope is the fixed meaning; the mechanisms are a face, a change of light, a living thing growing in a broken place, and another person's reassuring touch. Two of the four are deliberate multi-variable recipes — the sunrise and the neglected corner change the setting as well as the cue — so read them as combinations, not as single changes.
observe: Facial expression: brows gently raised, eyes bright and lifted toward something above the frame, the beginning of a smile.

First light: early sunrise light enters the café window as she turns toward it, the room still quiet. New growth: a small green seedling sprouts in a cracked cup on the table of a neglected, dusty café corner while she looks at it.
A helping hand: she offers a reassuring hand on her companion's shoulder — hope delivered by another person.
groups.meaning: Hope can be expressed by a face, promised by morning light, symbolized by new growth, or given by someone else's support.
groups.alternatives: Sunrise and seedlings are hopeful in many traditions but not automatically — for some viewers morning light simply means morning, and hope carried by symbols depends on the culture that taught the symbol.
concepts: Part II — light and time of day
groups.prompt_tip: Choose a concrete hope mechanism — 'first sunrise light through the window as she turns toward it' — and say what stays quiet around it, so the cue has room to read.

groups.title: Vulnerability, four ways
groups.fixed: The intended meaning (vulnerability) stays fixed; the visual mechanism changes.
groups.learn: Vulnerability is the fixed meaning; the mechanisms are a closed body, sheer scale, a looming second person, and a damaged treasured object. Compare how differently each route feels — defensive, exposed, threatened, or grieving — under the same one-word brief.
observe: Closed body language: arms crossed tightly. Scale and space: she is shown small in a vast empty warm-gray studio, in a wide shot with generous negative space on every side.

groups.meaning: Vulnerability can be a posture of self-protection, a figure diminished by space, a power imbalance between two people, or grief over something broken.
groups.alternatives: Crossed arms can read as defiance, or simply as feeling cold, rather than vulnerability, and a small figure in a big space could read as freedom — the surrounding cues, not the single gesture, settle the reading.
concepts: Part II — scale and negative space
groups.prompt_tip: Specify the vulnerability route — 'she stands small in a vast empty space, wide shot, nothing else in frame' — because 'vulnerable' alone usually returns only a sad face.

lessons.title: Semantic experiment B — Same visual element, different meanings
lessons.objective: Show that visual elements have no fixed universal meaning; context decides.
lessons.source_note: Supplementary semantic experiments (2026-11-26).
lessons.intro: This lesson runs the same experiment four times: hold one visual element still — red, darkness, an empty chair, a smile — and change everything around it. Each time, the meaning changes with the context, which is exactly the point: no visual element carries a fixed, universal meaning of its own. When you catch yourself thinking “red means danger” or “darkness means fear,” these plates are the counter-evidence.
lessons.exercise: Take the red plates: cover the captions and sort them by meaning. Which visual evidence did you actually use?
lessons.exercise_answer: The red element is constant across all four plates, so it cannot be the evidence. What you actually sorted by was the expression, the props, and the situation around the red — which is the lesson: the meaning was never in the color.

groups.title: Red, four meanings
groups.fixed: The element (red) stays; context changes its meaning.
groups.learn: Red is the same color in all four plates, yet it reads as romance, danger, celebration, and authority. What changes is the situation around the color, not the color itself — a color has no dictionary definition and borrows its meaning from the scene it appears in.
observe: In the romance plate, the red is a single rose in a small vase on the table, and TSMC looks at it with a soft, slight smile.
In the danger plate, red arrives as a deep warning glow spilling through the café window, and she sits tense and guarded, watching it.
Red lanterns and a red banner make the celebration plate, while a deep crimson backdrop drape behind her formal, centered stance makes the authority plate.
groups.meaning: The intended lesson is that red's meaning is supplied by context: a rose, a warning light, festival decorations, and a formal backdrop each recruit the same color for a different message.
groups.alternatives: The crimson-drape plate could also be read as ceremony or performance rather than authority, since a formal backdrop belongs to stages as well as to power.
concepts: Part II — dominant, secondary and accent colors
Part III — symbols and cultural meaning
groups.prompt_tip: Name the object and the situation, not just the color: ask for “a single red rose in a vase on the table, she smiles softly at it” rather than “a romantic red scene.”

groups.title: Darkness, four meanings
groups.fixed: The element (darkness) stays; context changes its meaning.
groups.learn: All four plates are dark, but the darkness means fear in one, privacy in another, intimacy in a third, and peaceful solitude in the fourth. Note that this group works differently from the others in this lesson: to change what the darkness means, the lighting itself had to change — this is a multi-variable recipe, not one held element with a new label.
observe: In the fear plate, the café is in near darkness with one distant light, and TSMC sits rigid, eyes wide toward the dark entrance.
In the privacy plate she reads relaxed in a dim, enclosed corner with a small lamp nearby; in the intimacy plate, she and ASML lean toward each other in dim warm lamplight, speaking quietly.
In the solitude plate, she sits calmly by the café window in blue evening dimness, tea in hand, at ease alone.
groups.meaning: The intended lesson is that darkness is a container, not a message: what fills it — a threat, a book, a companion, or quiet — decides what it means.
groups.alternatives: The peaceful-solitude plate could be read as loneliness instead, especially by a viewer who expects a café scene to be social; her relaxed posture and ease are the evidence against that reading.
concepts: Part II — light side and shadow side
Part III — atmosphere and emotional context
groups.prompt_tip: Describe the light source and her reaction to the dark, not just “dark scene”: “she reads calmly by a small lamp in a dim corner” produces privacy, while “she sits rigid, eyes wide toward a dark doorway” produces fear.

groups.title: An empty chair, four meanings
groups.fixed: The element (an empty chair) stays; context changes its meaning.
groups.learn: An empty chair is just furniture until the scene tells you why it is empty. Across these plates, the same absence reads as someone expected, someone lost, someone who just left, and someone deliberately shut out.
observe: In the expected plate, the empty seat has an untouched cup waiting in front of it, and she watches the seat.

In the lost plate, a visitor's coat still drapes over the empty chair's back while she gazes at it quietly, hands still; in the just-left plate, the chair is pulled out and a second cup is still steaming.
In the exclusion plate, TSMC and ASML talk together at the table while a third chair stands apart, turned away from them and left outside their circle.
groups.meaning: The intended lesson is that absence becomes a story only when traces — a waiting cup, a left-behind coat, a turned-away chair — tell the viewer what kind of absence it is.
groups.alternatives: The just-left plate could also be read as expectation, since a steaming cup might be waiting for someone about to sit down rather than left by someone who has gone.
concepts: Part III — props and environmental storytelling
Part II — composition and negative space
groups.prompt_tip: Give the empty chair a trace: ask for “an empty chair with a coat draped over its back, her gaze resting on it” so the absence has a specific story instead of reading as an unfinished scene.

groups.title: A smile, four meanings
groups.fixed: The element (a smile) stays; context changes its meaning.
groups.learn: All four portraits smile, but the smile is the least informative part of each face. The eyes, brows, jaw, and gaze direction around the mouth decide whether the same smile reads as genuine happiness, politeness, concealed hostility, or nervousness.
observe: In the genuine plate, the smile is broad and relaxed, with raised cheeks joining the mouth.
In the politeness plate, the mouth smiles while the eyes stay visibly tense.

In the hostility plate, the smile is held with narrowed eyes, a tight jaw, and one mouth corner pulled harder than the other; in the nervousness plate, raised tense brows and lips pressed thin at one side accompany a slightly averted gaze.
groups.meaning: The intended lesson is that a smile is a family of expressions, not a single signal: the whole face votes on what it means.
groups.alternatives: The politeness plate could be read as discomfort or strain rather than courtesy — politeness is the social interpretation we give a smile that the eyes do not join.
concepts: Part III — emotional intensity and concealment
groups.prompt_tip: Prompt the whole face, not the mouth: “a smile with narrowed eyes and a tight jaw” reads as concealed hostility, while “a broad smile with raised cheeks” reads as genuine happiness.

lessons.title: Semantic experiment C — Same image, different context
lessons.objective: Show that meaning can come from outside the picture: the same image reads differently under different captions.
lessons.source_note: Supplementary semantic experiments (2026-11-26); images reused unchanged.
lessons.intro: In this experiment the pictures do not change at all — the same four images appear exactly as they did earlier in the course. What changes is the caption underneath each one, and with each new caption the same face tells a different story. A caption is not hidden inside the image; it is narrative context that text — and the viewer — supplies from outside the picture.
lessons.exercise: Read one picture under all three captions. Which caption was hardest to believe, and what in the picture resisted it?
lessons.exercise_answer: Pictures constrain captions without determining them: a caption that fights the visible evidence — her solitude, her stillness, the sealed envelope — feels wrong even though no caption can be proved from the image alone. Those resistance points are real evidence; note them.

groups.title: One picture, three stories
groups.fixed: The picture never changes; only the page-rendered caption changes.
groups.learn: Each picture here is shown under three different captions, and each caption makes the same expression tell a different story. The image constrains which captions can survive, but it never picks one by itself — captions are narrative context supplied by the text and the viewer, not information contained in the picture.
observe: The café control picture stays identical while its captions move from arriving early for a first meeting, to returning to a favorite café alone, to finally resting after ten years of work.
In the staging picture, the sealed envelope on the table supports all three of its captions: a long-awaited letter, a disappointment she already knows, or a letter left on the wrong table.

The lost-in-thought plate's unfocused distant gaze fits rehearsing a speech, deciding to resign, and not noticing cold tea equally well; the nostalgic plate's old photograph near the cup can be the café's first day, a friend who will not return, or a stranger's picture found in a book.
groups.meaning: The intended lesson is that the same visual evidence can honestly support several stories, and the caption — supplied from outside the image — is what selects one of them.
groups.alternatives: A caption can also fail: if one claimed she was celebrating loudly with friends, these solitary, still pictures would push back — context steers meaning, but it cannot override everything visible.
groups.prompt_tip: When you generate an image for a story, write the caption first and prompt for the evidence it needs: “she gazes unfocused into the distance, her tea untouched” leaves room for several captions, while a specific prop narrows the story down.

It was the first morning she returned to their favorite café alone.
After ten years of work, she could finally sit down and rest.
C04: The letter she had waited months for was finally here.
She already knew what was inside, and it would change nothing.
Someone had left it on the wrong table — it was never meant for her.
l05-g03-v04: She was rehearsing exactly what she would say when he arrived.
She had just decided to leave the company she had built her life around.
Her tea had gone cold an hour ago; she had not noticed.
l13-g01-v04: The photograph showed the café's first day, forty years ago.
She kept the photo of the friend who would not be coming back.

lessons.title: Semantic experiment D — Same scene, different narrative intent
lessons.objective: Show that genre lives in behavior, props and emphasis — not in a style filter.
lessons.source_note: Supplementary semantic experiments (2026-11-26).
lessons.intro: Five plates, one meeting: TSMC and ASML sit at the same café table, in the same two-shot, drawn in exactly the same style. Yet one plate is a romance, one a psychological thriller, one a comedy, one a corporate drama, and one a story about grief. The genre was changed by hands, props, and glances — genre is not a filter, and none of these plates uses a different color grade or rendering style.
lessons.exercise: Which of the five versions could you turn into another genre by changing only props? Which needs behavior to change?
lessons.exercise_answer: Props carry setting and stakes — swapping the flower for a contract moves romance toward corporate drama. Relationships live in behavior and gaze, though: the grief version's silence and quietly supportive hand cannot be produced by props alone.

groups.title: One meeting, five genres
groups.fixed: Same café two-shot: TSMC screen left, ASML screen right, meeting at the table. Change behavior, props and emphasis only — never the rendering style or color grade.
groups.learn: Genre lives in behavior, props, and emphasis. With the camera, the café, and the drawing style held constant, each version of this one meeting becomes a different kind of story purely through what the two people do and what sits on the table between them.
observe: In the romance, ASML offers TSMC a single small flower across the table; both smile shyly, gazes meeting, cups forgotten.

In the thriller, ASML slides a folded note across the table and TSMC stares at it without touching it, both tense; in the comedy, ASML proudly presents an absurdly tall stack of pancakes while TSMC stares in disbelief, spoon paused mid-air.

In the corporate drama, a contract and a wafer case lie on the table between two upright, formal, guarded negotiators with locked gazes; in the grief story, the two sit in silence with an untouched second cup between them, ASML's hand resting near TSMC's in quiet support.
groups.meaning: The intended lesson is that genre is a set of storytelling decisions — what people want, fear, hide, or offer — expressed through behavior and props, not a visual filter applied afterward.
groups.alternatives: The thriller plate could be read as a serious business handover rather than a threat, since a folded note stays ambiguous until someone tells you what is written on it.
concepts: Part III — genre and narrative framing
Part II — emphasis and focal point
groups.prompt_tip: Ask for the genre's behavior, not its name: “she slides a folded note across the table; the other stares at it without touching it, both tense” produces a thriller more reliably than the words “psychological thriller scene.”

lessons.title: Semantic experiment E — Intended vs perceived meaning
lessons.objective: Practice interpreting an image before the intended meaning is revealed, and see why viewers disagree.
lessons.source_note: Supplementary semantic experiments (2026-11-26); quiz mode supported.
lessons.intro: Each group in this lesson is a pair of plates prompted for two neighboring meanings — confidence and arrogance, calmness and indifference, and so on. The quiz hides the intended readings so you can interpret each plate first; the reveal then shows what the prompt actually asked for. Expect to disagree with the reveal sometimes — that disagreement is the lesson, because an image succeeds when its intended audience takes away the intended meaning, not merely when a prompt was followed.
lessons.exercise: For one pair, write the prompt change you would make to push the first reading further from the second.
lessons.exercise_answer: Small changes do the work: gaze direction, distance between figures, and hand tension all move a reading without changing the scene. There is no objectively correct answer — check your change against how a fresh viewer actually reads the result.

groups.title: Confidence vs arrogance
groups.fixed: Two readings of similar cues; neither reading is scored as objectively correct.
groups.learn: Confidence and arrogance use nearly the same body — upright, open, self-assured. This pair shows how small adjustments to the chin, the gaze, and the hands tip the same assurance into one reading or the other.
observe: In the first plate, her torso is upright with shoulders relaxed back — assurance without tension.
In the second plate, her chin is raised high and her gaze is directed down toward the viewer.
The second plate adds one hand dismissively at her waist and her weight leaned back.
groups.meaning: The first plate was prompted to be read as confidence and the second as arrogance; both readings are presented neutrally, and either plate may land differently for different viewers.
groups.alternatives: Neither reading is objectively correct — what matters is which one the intended audience actually takes away.
concepts: Part II — viewpoint and camera angle
groups.prompt_tip: To ask for confidence without arrogance, prompt “upright posture, shoulders relaxed, level gaze”; adding “chin raised, looking down at the viewer” deliberately crosses into arrogance.

groups.title: Authority vs intimidation
groups.fixed: Two readings of similar cues; neither reading is scored as objectively correct.
groups.learn: Authority and intimidation both arrange people into higher and lower positions. Whether the arrangement reads as legitimate leadership or as a threat depends on the lower person's ease — and on whether the higher person's power falls across them like a shadow.
observe: In the first plate, TSMC gives calm instructions while her companion attends to her.
In the second plate, TSMC stands while ASML remains seated, so the height difference is built into the furniture.
In the second plate, TSMC's long shadow falls across the table, and ASML leans back slightly.
